extracted.intended_audience: Public Information Officers (PIOs) and Assistant PIOs / incident information staff (emergency response communicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for preparing press releases, fact sheets, and conducting media relations during incidents (emergencies/hazmat events), aimed at PIOs and assistant PIOs supporting an Incident Management Team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't take it personally
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter is neither your enemy nor your friend; he/she is an intermediary between you and the people you need to reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let ego drive interactions with reporters. Treat journalists as conduits to the public rather than opponents or allies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control what you can
rubrics_metrics.description: Release the bad news yourself—before some reporter digs it up. Use your selective availability to reporters as a tool. Set ground rules every time you talk. If the public isn't buying your message, change it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively manage timing and framing of information. Use controlled access and agreed-upon boundaries during interviews; adjust messaging when it proves ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know whom you're dealing with
rubrics_metrics.description: The press is not monolithic. TV is different from print, magazines are different from newspapers, and particular outlets differ widely. Do your homework on journalists before you talk to them, reviewing their past work and talking to other executives they have covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor approach to medium and individual reporter; research past coverage and reputation to anticipate style, priorities, and likely angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid TV unless comfortable; use sound bites
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid TV unless you feel free to speak candidly. Even then, learn to present your views in the 10-second sound bites that are the building blocks of TV stories. Use simple, declarative sentences and ignore subtleties. Whenever possible, favor live TV shows over those that can edit your remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare concise sound bites; prefer live broadcasts when you want to prevent selective editing. Simplify language for broadcast; practice delivering short, clear statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be human
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters—and the public—usually will be more sympathetic to a person than a corporation. If you can do it without lying or making an ass of yourself, reveal yourself as a person with feelings: your mistakes will as likely be forgiven as criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate personal expression to build credibility and relatability; aim to be judged on a human scale without compromising facts or professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop media lists (target vs secondary) — anti-pattern when misused
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop essential and nonessential media lists. Set up your list, work only with the target market editors, and ignore inquiries from all other publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This item appears under 'Ways to Make Enemies in the Press' as an example of poor behavior when you deliberately ignore other interested outlets. Best practice: maintain prioritized lists but do not reflexively dismiss legitimate inquiries from secondary outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put up road blocks to reporters — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a priority list of editors that you will talk with and those that your PR person should handle. For frivolous inquiries, have someone else handle them so most requests fall into that category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a poor practice. Creating unnecessary barriers or deflecting reporters damages relationships; instead triage respectfully and respond appropriately to legitimate inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return calls in due course (delayed response tactic) — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it obvious that reporters' time isn't as important as yours; return calls when you get around to it (timing suggestions given: 6:00 pm for dailies, Friday/Monday 2:00 pm for weeklies, etc.), respond with 'no comment' or say you don't have information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a way to make enemies. Best practice is timely, respectful responses aligned to reporters' deadlines and needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scream when a story isn't 100 percent positive — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reporter prints something negative, call the publisher and demand a retraction or firing; follow up with letters to publisher, editor, reporter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This overreactive tactic is listed as bad practice. Appropriate responses should be measured, fact-based correction requests or clarifications, not personal attacks or public demands for firing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strike back (embargo/withdraw advertising) — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Place an embargo on the guilty medium by not responding to inquiries or pulling advertising/information because the medium is 'no longer good' for reaching customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an adversarial response that harms long-term relationships. Use measured commercial decisions and pursue constructive engagement instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk down to reporters (use only one-syllable words) — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Make certain reporters know you know more about the subject; talk down, explain each point repeatedly, let them know your time is more valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also listed as a way to make enemies. Treat reporters with respect; condescension damages credibility and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick and choose opportunities to avoid long-term relationships — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperate with the press when you need immediate coverage, but avoid developing open lines of communication and strong long-term relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term opportunism undermines trust. Build long-term relationships where beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insist that everything be cleared / demand pre-publication review — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Remind the reporter that everything must be cleared through PR or legal before it can be used; demand the right to review copy before printing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presented as a way to make enemies. While technical-accuracy checks are sometimes acceptable, demanding blanket pre-publication approval is unrealistic and damages relations. If copy review is permitted, limit it to factual/technical checks and follow agreed protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have all queries and responses screened — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Require that all questions and answers go through PR so responses are coached and cleaned up to show you in the best light or say nothing at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a negative practice. Screening is appropriate for coordination and safety, but heavy-handed filtering that prevents transparency will erode trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give multiple exclusives — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiate an exclusive with a top medium, then give the same 'exclusive' to two or three other outlets so each feels privileged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is flagged as a way to make enemies. Honor exclusivity agreements or be transparent about simultaneous releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torpedo the energetic reporter — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reporter wants to expand a story, call other reporters and give them the same information to dilute the original reporter's opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This undermines reporters and is bad practice. Collaborate with interested reporters in good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie weak stories to advertising — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the reporter you're a big advertiser and expect major treatment; send the story along with your advertising order and ask media rep to do legwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using advertising as leverage for editorial favor is unethical and damages credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand clippings of coverage — anti-pattern (when done abusively)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remind editors every time you send a release that you need clippings when the piece is printed; insist on printed clippings to 'make certain' they're doing a good job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a way to make enemies, this item suggests overbearing behavior. Reasonable post-publication monitoring is fine; do not harass outlets for clippings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise (press release)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors, webmasters, etc. receive hundreds of press releases and appreciate releases that are brief and to the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep releases short; prioritize essential facts and avoid unnecessary length or padding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-written (press release)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid bad spelling, poor grammar, and politically motivated, illogical, or unsubstantiated claims—the quickest way to end up in the wastebasket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofread carefully; ensure logical structure and avoid partisan or speculative language. Professional writing increases pickup probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual (press release)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stick to logical and substantiated claims, avoiding statements of belief (e.g., 'we're the best, the cheapest, etc.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support assertions with verifiable facts and sources; avoid hyperbole and subjective marketing claims presented as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest (press release)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid padded quotes by incident personnel; even expert quotes can come across as biased. If personnel quotes are used, stick to pure incident facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use candid, factual quotes and avoid spin. Overly promotional or rhetorical quotes reduce credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely (press release)
rubrics_metrics.description: If your press release isn’t topical based on incident events, an editor might consider it a sidebar or special-interest feature—but don’t stretch it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Release timing matters—match distribution to newsworthiness and current incident developments; avoid forcing relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define target audience and desired takeaway
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing, decide: Who is the preferred audience (public, evacuees, potential contractors)? What do you want your target audience to take away from your press release?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor content, tone, and call-to-action to the specific audience and clear communication objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what the release provides
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what your press release provides (e.g., information on evacuations, injuries, fatalities, incident progress, damage, property loss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the specific, actionable information the audience needs; avoid extraneous material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide the tone of your press release (e.g., imminent danger, danger is passed, incident nearly over, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone must match incident status and audience needs—convey urgency or reassurance as appropriate without understatement or alarmism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate pitfalls and avoid sensitive topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of possible pitfalls of incident tactics or areas to avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screen for legal, safety, or operational sensitivities; coordinate with incident command and legal advisors as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: State clear objectives for the release
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide what you want to accomplish (e.g., increase public awareness, disseminate information, provide timely warnings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make each release serve a clear communicative purpose and include measurable calls-to-action when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead must answer journalism's basic tenets (5 W's + How)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the press release lead addresses Who, What, When, Where, Why, How in pyramid writing style; put good stuff in the first paragraph and allow cutting from the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure releases so editors can trim bottom material without losing core facts. Lead with the most newsworthy facts and the essential details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare a concise fact sheet (no reading from notes on camera)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a fact sheet as talking points (not a written press release); you will not be allowed to read from notes on camera. Be very familiar with your facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize accuracy and brevity when preparing fact sheets. Practice delivering talking points from memory to maintain eye contact and credibility on camera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-sheet prep: three guiding questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing your fact sheet, answer: (1) What are the facts you can report? (2) What should you strive to do during this interview? (3) What are your talking points?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to focus content and objectives for each interview; limit talk tracks to factual, approved information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview practice: demonstrate live interview techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should demonstrate techniques necessary to effectively handle live interviews and determine incident information to share with the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice under realistic conditions (timed, role-play) and use debriefing/critique of recorded interviews to improve performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate approvals for releases (PIO/Assistant PIO role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assistant PIOs should edit and obtain approval from the Lead Public Information Officer for news releases and other for-release documents. In the absence of the Lead PIO, release information in accordance with the Incident Commander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish clear sign-off procedures and escalation paths for timely, authorized releases during an incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather, manage, and analyze incident information
rubrics_metrics.description: Assistant PIOs and Internal Communications staff must gather, manage, and analyze information from all parts of the Incident Command Post and display information for use in the Information Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement systems to collect, verify, and present incident data (situation updates, IAPs, health/safety bulletins) that inform press releases and public messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce communication products (talking points, briefings, releases, PSAs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop communication and outreach products based on information from the Communications Unit, such as talking points, briefings, flyers, fact sheets, news releases, and public service announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consistency and accuracy across all products; adapt format and detail to channel/audience needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish information-flow systems and internal communication centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish and implement systems to manage the flow of information; maintain internal information centers (bulletin boards, posted IAPs, local news articles, incident status updates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralize information to avoid duplication, ensure frontline and internal staff have current, consistent facts to support external communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate external communications and stakeholder monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Assistant PIO for External Communications manages distribution of information, coordinates meetings/interviews, monitors community concerns, and advises Lead PIO about community information needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor media and community sentiment; adjust messaging and outreach strategies to address misinformation and stakeholder needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: External comms tasks: prepare speakers, conduct conferences, analyze clips
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare speakers prior to interviews; conduct news conferences and town meetings; analyze print and electronic news clips; escort the media; identify misinformation or rumors that may affect the response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide media training, schedule and prepare spokespeople, and conduct media monitoring to inform corrections or follow-up releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish and manage a Joint Information Center (JIC) if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Assistant PIOs may establish and manage a Joint Information Center to coordinate information across agencies and the Incident Command structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a JIC to centralize multi-agency messaging, reduce duplication, and present unified, consistent public information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure documentation and cost/accounting (administrative duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supervise operational and administrative activities, set staff work hours/schedules, ensure all costs are accounted, and maintain an ICS Form 214 Activity Log.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain administrative discipline to support after-action reviews, reimbursements, and accountability for information operations.
